The best 3-qubit chain on Garnet is QB11-QB12-QB7. QB12 sits in the middle. I read Garnet's current default calibration, which is set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d. That set lists an interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) fidelity for each of Garnet's 30 CZ pairs. The pair QB11-QB12 has a fidelity of 0.999454. The pair QB12-QB7 has a fidelity of 0.999066. Their product is 0.998520, which is the highest of any connected chain. The second best is QB11-QB12-QB17, with a product of 0.998175.

What I ran: I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit by hand from IQM's native gates and named those three physical qubits directly. The circuit first puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Two CZ gates then link QB12 to QB11 and QB12 to QB7. Single-qubit rotations around the CZ gates turn each CZ into a CNOT. The job then measured all three qubits. I read the circuit back from the server. It has exactly 2 CZ gates, on (QB12, QB11) and (QB12, QB7). The measured qubits are QB11, QB12, and QB7. A noise-free simulation of this exact gate list gives 000 half the time and 111 half the time.

Results: Job 01a16483-7170-722f-be73-b1ce986c01a0 ran 200 shots on garnet:mock. Each bitstring lists QB11, QB12, QB7 in that order. The counts were 000: 45, 011: 57, 100: 51, and 111: 47. The mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bits, so the outcomes 011 and 100 show up even though a perfect GHZ state never gives them. The mock run shows that the circuit is valid and that the server accepts it on these qubits. It does not show entanglement. On real Garnet you would expect mostly 000 and 111.

The principle: a GHZ state puts all three qubits into one shared state. Each qubit on its own looks random, but all three always agree. Every CZ gate adds a small error. Picking the chain whose two CZ fidelities have the highest product gives the circuit the best chance of keeping that agreement. The mock job cost 0 credits.
